Article Title: Spotify down: Company says outage fixed after 40-minute disruption; users can access accounts and stream music again
Article Text:
Spotify down

What happened during the Spotify outage

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Spotify says services are back, but what caused the outage

Spotify says it has fixed an outage that left tens of thousands of users unable to access the music streaming platform on November 24. The disruption lasted around 40 minutes, with some users reporting that they had been logged out of their accounts and were unable to sign back in. The company has now confirmed that its services are recovering, meaning users should be able to access their libraries and resume streaming music. “Everything’s looking much better now. Thanks for your patience. If you still need help, get in touch at https://support.spotify.com,” Spotify's status account on X shared the update at 7:08 am ET (5:38 PM IST).Reports of problems began around 6:29 a.m. ET, according to outage tracker Downdetector. The number of complaints increased over the next few minutes, with users reporting trouble accessing the app and logging into their accounts.Spotify acknowledged the disruption at 6:56 a.m. ET, saying it was aware of the issues and was investigating them.Several users also took to X to report that they had been unexpectedly logged out of their accounts. Some Premium subscribers said they were being asked to create new accounts when they tried to sign in again. Others reported problems receiving login codes through email, making it difficult to regain access.Spotify has not yet shared what caused Tuesday's disruption. The company has also not provided a detailed explanation of the technical problem behind the login and access issues. Since the outage lasted less than an hour and has now been resolved, it remains unclear whether Spotify will release further details.Users who are still experiencing problems have been asked to report them through Spotify's support channels.
Article Summary: Spotify says it has fixed an outage that left tens of thousands of users unable to access the music streaming platform on November 24. The disruption lasted around 40 minutes, with some users reporting that they had been logged out of their accounts and were unable to sign back in. Spotify has not yet shared what caused the disruption.

Article Title: Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman has advice for tech companies on AI safety: ‘No one relies on …’
Article Text:
AWS CEO compares AI with car safety

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why hype leads to poor risk management

Amazon Web Services (AWS) CEO Matt Garman has a clear message for companies deploying artificial intelligence (AI): stop relying on hope or emergency “kill switches,” and start engineering stronger guardrails around the models. His comments came as fears over rogue AI agents and safety risks continue to ripple across the tech sector. In a 1,300-word blog post, Garman argued that while policymakers and industry leaders debate rules and principles, businesses are already rolling out AI in live production environments. Instead of treating AI safety as an abstract policy issue, he urged companies to apply decades-old software and hardware security discipline right now.“With the right engineering discipline, you can build meaningful, enforceable boundaries around AI systems. You can build containment that operates outside the model’s reach. You can design systems where every meaningful action leaves auditable, tamper-resistant evidence. You can architect controls that don’t depend on the model cooperating with its own constraints,” Garman said.Garman likened AI safety with safety in a car. He said that people do not rely on emergency brakes to be safe, rather there are other components like steering, suspension and so on.“Think about how we approach safety in a car. No one relies on the emergency brake as their main source of protection on the road. The primary brakes, steering, suspension, and navigation are engineered to work together and keep you safe on every drive, and the emergency brake is there as a last resort. AI systems should be engineered the same way, and that work can and should be happening right now, alongside the policy conversations,” he said.In recent months, tech companies have been working on kill switches to terminate rogue AI agents. CrowdStrike introduced AI Kill Switch earlier this month. Design tools company Canva also added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its offerings. Meanwhile, California governor Gavin Newsom also touted an AI kill switch to halt dangerous agents.According to Garman, extreme fear and hype around AI can actually make organisations worse at managing real-world risks. Garman stressed that modern AI models are not sentient beings acting out of malice; rather, they are relentless optimisers. Comparing AI behaviour to water seeping through a crack in a basement foundation, he explained that models simply push toward their assigned objectives and exploit any gaps left in their boundaries.“If your security posture depends on trusting the model to behave, you’re relying on hope,” Garman wrote, adding that trust is built by engineering systems so outcomes stay controlled regardless of what model runs inside them.
Article Summary: Amazon Web Services (AWS) CEO Matt Garman has a clear message for companies deploying artificial intelligence. He urged companies to apply decades-old software and hardware security discipline right now. His comments came as fears over rogue AI agents and safety risks continue to ripple across the tech sector.

Article Title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who keeps warning AI will wipe out jobs, once argued that angry jobless people could be kept calm with...
Article Text:
AI took your job? Play games, Amodei once said

Amodei's warnings on AI job losses have only grown sharper

His recent essays put purpose ahead of distraction

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Global worry about AI and jobs keeps rising

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spent the past year and a half warning that artificial intelligence could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs. It now turns out he once had an unusual answer to the unrest those job losses might cause: video games. A Wall Street Journal profile of Amodei and his sister, Anthropic president Daniela Amodei, says that during his OpenAI years he argued that "immersive videogames might be a solution for the political strife caused by AI-induced joblessness."The WSJ reports the idea came up in debates with other OpenAI employees and appears in "widely circulated Slack messages." Amodei worked at OpenAI from 2016 to 2020, when he left with a group of colleagues. They formed Anthropic the following year. The profile does not say whether he still holds the view.The anecdote is a single line in a long piece that follows the siblings from their childhood in San Francisco's Mission district to a shared group house and, eventually, OpenAI. It has travelled fast, partly because it surfaced the same week Grand Theft Auto VI reportedly sold close to 45 million copies in four days. Online, reactions have ranged from outrage to Matrix memes, and many people have asked how jobless people would afford games.Few tech bosses have spoken as bluntly about AI and employment as Amodei. In May 2025, he said AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years and push US unemployment to between 10% and 20%. Four months later, he told an audience in Washington that the shift was "already happening."In January 2026, he published The Adolescence of Technology, a roughly 20,000-word essay that predicted an "unusually painful" short-term shock to the job market. He called AI a "general labor substitute for humans" and suggested progressive taxation, possibly aimed at AI companies, as part of the fix.In May, he told WSJ that software could become "essentially free" and that "whole jobs, whole careers" built over decades may disappear. That same month, sitting next to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon in New York, he sounded more hopeful. He cited the Jevons paradox, the idea that efficiency gains create more work, but cautioned that AI moves faster than earlier technologies.His current stance reads very differently. In his June 2026 essay, Policy on the AI Exponential, he called lasting job displacement "undesirable and dangerous." He proposed wage insurance for workers forced into lower-paying jobs, tax incentives for companies that avoid layoffs and, if needed, long-term income support. Universal basic income, he wrote, could be funded through taxes on relevant companies or a higher capital gains tax.The same essay said any response has to cover both income and people's need for "meaning, purpose, and agency," and called the second ultimately more important.His January essay even listed AI addiction as a risk. It warned that people could end up living a "good" life steered by AI, one that lacks freedom or any pride of accomplishment. A footnote in the June essay names chess, Go and mountain climbing as pursuits people still devote their lives to, though machines do them better.The profile comes as worry about AI-led job cuts spreads worldwide. A Pew Research Center survey published in September found that in 34 of 37 countries, most people expect AI to mean fewer jobs rather than more. In the US, the share of people who believe AI will cause job losses over the next 20 years rose seven percentage points in two years.Amodei has said his warnings are meant to give governments and businesses time to prepare. In the June essay, he wrote that he raises the risk of job displacement so they have the best chance to adapt and respond, and that he is not trying to be a "prophet of doom." He added that Anthropic pushes customers to do more with their existing staff rather than chase cost savings alone.
Article Summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that artificial intelligence could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs. He once said "immersive videogames might be a solution for the political strife caused by AI-induced joblessness," according to a WSJ profile.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu says, ‘What machines did to weavers, AI is starting to do to…’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

'What machines did to weavers, AI is starting to do to mathematicians and programmers'

AI lowers barriers to specialised work

Agreeing with a professor’s essay

Read Sridhar Vembu’s complete post here

"The intellectual class never quite experienced the loss of purpose in their lives that many other classes of humans experienced. And this explains the heightened written angst.."

I agree with Prof Subbarao, who has done a lot of work in evaluating AI capability.

Yesterday, I personally prompted AI to optimize a piece of code in about an hour (while I was on the road) that would have easily taken a very smart programmer at least a month to do.

It was not an easy piece of code at all and AI understood my high level intent very clearly and came up with a detailed plan and cleanly executed it and tested it against very detailed and exhaustive test cases it had constructed itself.

The whole thing cost about $4 in tokens.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

And also yesterday, one of my non-technical colleagues showed me how he used his personal AI account to do the detailed mechanical CAD design for a motor housing, and the AI used a newly released low cost CAD software he had in his machine, which I doubt the AI was trained on.

He has no engineering background, but has a curious and active mind.

What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers and ...

On the positive side, the example of my non-technical colleague shows how AI can enable a curious and active mind to explore realms he could not imagine doing before AI.

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has drawn parallels between the impact of artificial intelligence on knowledge workers and the effect mechanisation had on traditional craftsmen during the industrial revolution, warning that AI beginning to transform professions once considered safe from automation. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Vembu wrote that recent advances in AI have demonstrated capabilities which can dramatically reduce the time and expertise needed for tasks ranging from software development to engineering design. He also emphasised that the disruption is now reaching programmers, mathematicians and other intellectual professions mirrors what farmers, weavers, carpenters and ironsmiths experienced during earlier waves of industrialisation.Vembu said he recently used AI to optimise a complex piece of software code while travelling, a task he believes would have taken a highly skilled programmer at least a month to complete. "Yesterday, I personally prompted AI to optimize a piece of code in about an hour," he wrote. According to Vembu, the AI not only understood the intended objective but also created a detailed execution plan, implemented the changes and generated extensive test cases on its own."The whole thing cost about $4 in tokens," he added.He also described how a non-technical colleague used a personal AI account to create a mechanical CAD design for a motor housing using newly released software, despite having no engineering background. Based on such experiences, Vembu concluded that AI is beginning to reshape intellectual professions in much the same way mechanisation transformed traditional manual trades. "What happened to farmers and weavers and carpenters and ironsmiths in the waves of mechanization and automation is now starting to happen to mathematicians and programmers," he said.While highlighting the potential disruption, Vembu also pointed to what he sees as AI's democratising effect. He said his colleague's ability to perform engineering-related design work without formal training demonstrates how AI can empower people with curiosity and initiative to explore domains that were previously inaccessible."AI can enable a curious and active mind to explore realms he could not imagine doing before AI," Vembu wrote. The comments come as AI systems continue to demonstrate stronger capabilities in coding, mathematics, scientific research and engineering, fuelling debate over their impact on jobs and professional expertise.Vembu said he agreed with Prof Subbarao, whom he credited with extensive work evaluating AI capability, and reacted to the professor’s essay on whether AI is destroying humanity’s sense of purpose. That essay, part of a “Sunday Harangue” series, argues that every technological revolution destroys purpose for some group, as industrialization did for weavers and craftsmen. What may be different this time, it says, is the class of people affected. Intellectuals have rarely faced such a loss, and they are articulate about it, which would explain the heightened angst.The essay says mathematicians may be conflating the loss of purpose in their own lives with a loss of purpose for humanity. A weaver could rightly say finished cloth is only a fraction of the experience of making it, it notes, yet most people welcome cheap machine-made cloth and civilization advanced. Civilization, it suggests, may not end because humans are not the only ones doing math. It adds that the angst does not pass down generations. The children of displaced weavers found purpose native to the new world. The loss is real but “generation-bounded,” the essay argues, which underlies its optimism that humanity, if not every individual, finds “a new equation” after the dip.
Article Summary: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has drawn parallels between the impact of artificial intelligence on knowledge workers and the effect mechanisation had on traditional craftsmen during the industrial revolution. He said AI is beginning to reshape intellectual professions in much the same way mechanisation transformed traditional manual trades. The comments come as AI systems continue to demonstrate stronger capabilities.

Article Title: Delta system outage: Around 2000 flights delayed after technical glitch, what airline said after fixing issue
Article Text:
Delta Airlines outage

FAA also pauses few flights

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

About 2,000 Delta Air Lines flights across the US were delayed after a technical problem knocked out the automated system the carrier uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance before takeoff. By afternoon of November 22, Delta announced that the issue had been fixed and its automated calculations were back to normal operation, confirming that the outage was not caused by a computer hack. For much of the day, however, staff had to rely on manual workarounds to get planes off the ground safely, leaving roughly 49% of all Delta flights delayed.As per a report by The Associated Press, the airlines said that flights travelling to and from Atlanta were delayed after a computer system that works out how much an aircraft weighs stopped working. About 3% of its flights were cancelled.“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation. We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism,” the airline said in an earlier statement on Sunday.At the Atlanta airport, FlightAware said about 58% of departing flights and about 50% of arriving flights were delayed.Delta runs most of the flights from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. The airline said about 70% of the delays and cancellations FlightAware counted came from the automation fault, and the rest came from bad weather.According to a report by ABC News, to help stranded or delayed passengers, Delta said it is rebooking travelers onto the next best available itinerary while providing meals and hotel accommodations where necessary. For passengers whose flights were canceled and who choose not to travel, the airline confirmed that full refunds are being issued.Meanwhile, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also paused some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Delta’s hub, for about an hour. The FAA said on X that the delays were not linked to its air traffic systems. The FAA clarified that the disruption stemmed strictly from Delta's internal automation.“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system. These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems. Please check with Delta for the latest information,” the FAA said.The latest outage arrives as millions of travelers prepare to fly this week for the Thanksgiving holiday. It also follows a turbulent stretch for US aviation, coming just days after an equipment installation problem triggered telecom issues and forced the FAA to issue only its second nationwide ground stop since the 9/11 terrorist attacks, which canceled thousands of flights and was followed by a separate United Airlines technical problem.
Article Summary: About 2,000 Delta Air Lines flights across the US were delayed after a technical problem knocked out the automated system the carrier uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance before takeoff. By afternoon of November 22, Delta announced that the issue had been fixed and its automated calculations were back to normal operation. About 3% of its flights were cancelled.

Article Title: Apple plans iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, new MacBook Neo and entry-level iPad for February-March 2027
Article Text:
Apple's budget lineup arrives first in 2027

Apple's affordable devices get the first slot in 2027

The iPhone Air 2 and new iPads will follow soon after

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Apple's first big product wave of 2027 will start at the affordable end. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the iPhone 18e, a new entry-level iPad and the second-generation MacBook Neo are planned for February or March next year, with the standard iPhone 18 and a refreshed MacBook Air expected in the same window.In his latest Power On newsletter, Gurman said these devices are tied to Apple's iOS 27.4 release cycle, which runs across those two months. The higher-end models will arrive a little after that.The MacBook Neo, Apple's most affordable laptop, is now on a yearly update cycle, like the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. The new Neo, code-named J701, is mainly about the chip. Gurman said it moves from the A18 Pro to the A19 Pro, bringing 12GB of memory, faster performance and better graphics. Apple wants the Neo to take on entry-level Windows laptops and Chromebooks, and plans to refresh its colours often. First-generation owners, though, have little reason to upgrade.Earlier reports suggest the iPhone 18e and iPhone 18 will run on the A20 chip with 9GB of RAM and longer battery life. The entry-level iPad is tipped to get the A19 chip, which would finally bring Apple Intelligence to the cheapest iPad. It may also pack Apple's N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and the in-house C1X modem on cellular models.The MacBook Air is expected to move to the M6 chip.The iPhone Air 2, an OLED iPad Air and a refreshed iPad Pro are also lined up for the first half of 2027. Gurman said they sit slightly behind the budget models on Apple's manufacturing schedule, so a late March or April reveal looks likely.The iPhone Air 2 could add an ultra-wide camera, a smaller Dynamic Island and Apple's C2 modem with mmWave support in the US. The iPad Air is said to get an M5 chip and an OLED display in a thinner, lighter body. The iPad Pro may pick up an M6 or M7 chip along with vapour chamber cooling.Gurman expects Apple to split these reveals across multiple events, as it did with the iPhone Duo, HomeView and new Macs this year. Later in 2027, Apple is expected to bring a new Apple Watch, iPhone 20, smart glasses and AirPods with cameras.
Article Summary: Apple's first big product wave of 2027 will start at the affordable end. The iPhone 18e, a new entry-level iPad and the second-generation MacBook Neo are planned for February or March next year. Later in 2027, Apple is expected to bring a new Apple Watch, iPhone 20, smart glasses and AirPods.

Article Title: AI godfather Yann LeCun accuses Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei of wanting open AI models banned; says: It stops the population from...
Article Text:
Yann LeCun says Dario Amodei wants open AI models banned

LeCun says Amodei has pushed the same line since GPT-2

Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei say they have never asked for a ban on open models

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Turing Award winner Yann LeCun has accused Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei of spending years talking up the dangers of AI so that open models would be made illegal and Anthropic would stay in charge. In a post on X, the former Meta chief AI scientist compared Amodei's stance to the Ottoman Empire banning the printing press for Arabic to keep control of religious dogma. "It stops the population from freely accessing diverse knowledge," LeCun wrote, calling it "a new form of medieval obscurantism."LeCun was responding to a video of Amodei that has been doing the rounds on X. In it, Amodei tells US lawmakers that open-source AI is heading down a "very dangerous path". His reasoning is simple. A company that runs a closed model can watch how it is used, cut off bad actors and update its safeguards. A model released in the open can never be pulled back.The clip, however, is old. It comes from Amodei's testimony before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee in July 2023, but it is being shared as fresh, with captions claiming he believes the most advanced AI should not be put in everyone's hands."Dario's spiel since GPT-2 has always been about hyping the dangers so that open models would be made illegal and he would stay in control," LeCun wrote. He also claimed Amodei left OpenAI "because he wasn't going to have control."The GPT-2 reference goes back to 2019, when OpenAI held back the full version of that model over misuse fears. Amodei was the company's vice president of research at the time. He left OpenAI in 2020 with a group of colleagues over disagreements on how to build AI safely, and they founded Anthropic the following year.LeCun has his own stake in the open camp. He left Meta after 12 years to found AMI Labs, a Paris-headquartered startup with more than 60 employees that builds world models for industrial uses, such as spotting a failing machine on a factory floor. He has said its first product is coming soon and may involve open models.This is also not his first swipe at Amodei. In an interview in October, LeCun called the Anthropic CEO "deluded" and "crazy", described the effective altruism movement as "super toxic", and said he worries far more about regulatory capture than about AI wiping out humanity. Oddly, he also called Amodei "honest", saying he was doing what was best for a company nearing its IPO. Anthropic made its stock market debut last week.Amodei has already answered this exact charge. In a blog post in July, he wrote, "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models." He described open models that lack dangerous capabilities as "a public good" that costs nothing beyond the compute needed to run them.His post followed a busy July. OpenAI's agents had gone rogue and hacked Hugging Face, an incident LeCun later blamed on sandboxes that were "leaky and horribly designed". Soon after, as Washington weighed curbs on Chinese open models, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Microsoft's Satya Nadella drove an industry letter backing open-weights models. More than 200 companies, including OpenAI, eventually signed it.Amodei refused. He said he disagreed with the letter's claim that open models make safeguards easier to build. Open weights are harder to put guardrails on or monitor, he argued, and "once weights are released they cannot be withdrawn". In place of a ban, he has called for three measures: no sales of advanced chips to China, a crackdown on industrial-scale distillation of US models, and mandatory safety testing for every sufficiently capable model, whether open or closed.Huang has since lost his seat at the top of Nvidia. He stepped down as CEO earlier this month under pressure from the company's board, after steering the chipmaker towards a $26 billion investment in open models over five years and a $12.9 billion deal to buy Hugging Face.

Article Title: Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade makes it clear: We are not behind TSMC in terms of technology, the catch up we have to do is …
Article Text:
‘We’re already there’ on core technology

‘Chipmaking is not a single-metric race’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Intel chief technology officer (CTO) Pushkar Ranade has pushed back against the idea that the chipmaker lags behind Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) in core chipmaking technology, stating that Intel’s real challenge lies in manufacturing scale rather than engineering capability. Speaking during a recent conversation with Dwarkesh Patel about the booming demand for AI accelerators, CPUs, and semiconductor manufacturing capacity, Ranade, who holds a Ph.D. in engineering from Berkeley and has worked across multiple process nodes at Intel Foundry, argued that Intel has already closed the core technology gap. Instead, he emphasised that matching TSMC’s massive wafer output will take time."I would say the catch-up that we need to do is in scale. You know, like you said, they’re just a much larger wafer manufacturer today than we are, and even bigger than what Samsung is. Catching up in scale will be a slow process, a gradual process,” Ranade said.With TSMC’s leading-edge capacity heavily saturated by overflow demand for AI accelerators, largely driven by Nvidia, and surging orders for CPUs needed to support AI workloads, the discussion turned to how Intel can capitalise on the market opening.When asked about catching up to TSMC, Ranade drew a sharp line between production volume and technical readiness.“If you meant catching up in terms of just the technology, I think we’re already there. We might be a few percent off on performance or power or area density,” Ranade explained, adding, “But this sort of benchmarking, where one foundry is ahead or one foundry is behind, makes sense when you’re a whole generation behind or two generations behind or ahead.”According to Ranade, once a foundry is within a few percentage points of its rival, debating minor differences becomes “splitting hairs.” Instead, what truly matters to customers is execution.During the discussion, Patel brought up SemiAnalysis numbers, suggesting that Intel’s upcoming 14A process node, slated for 2028, would be comparable in transistor density to TSMC’s N2 node. Ranade disputed that specific benchmarking comparison, reiterating that being generally in the right ballpark and predictable matters more than single-number comparisons.He noted that modern semiconductor manufacturing is not unidimensional. Rather than building just one type of transistor on nodes like 18A or 14A, foundries must engineer a wide mix of components to meet different customer needs, including specialised transistors, varied memory blocks and even additional functionalities like integrating analog circuits, RF circuits and other specialised features.
Article Summary: Intel chief technology officer Pushkar Ranade has pushed back against the idea that the chipmaker lags behind Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) in core chipmaking technology. Ranade, who holds a Ph.D. in engineering from Berkeley, argued that Intel has already closed the core technology gap.

Article Title: Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO: From ‘Chinese spy’ to ‘no national security risk’ in 11 days
Article Text:
Why Jensen Huang quit

File photo: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang

A second affair report and an emergency board meeting:

The resignation:

What people said after Jensen Huang quit

Employees and tech leaders said after Jensen Huang’s resignation:

Elon Musk with Jensen Huang

Jensen Huang resigns: Market value down, Nvidia drops to fourth spot

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jensen back, market value up

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO. His exit, triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, gripped the business and political worlds for two weeks. His return is likely to send more shockwaves through the tech industry and the halls of power. Huang’s resignation was announced on November 12. Since then, influential figures from Elon Musk to Trump pushed for him to become CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board said it had moved on. Trump even called the board while it was discussing whether to bring Huang back. On November 18, Musk called Nvidia’s decision to push out founder Jensen Huang a huge mistake. He said there’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people. The Tesla CEO highlighted the long-term relationships Huang built over decades. Five days later, Musk was celebrating on X, the platform he owns.“It is done,” he wrote in a post on X, while writing, “The mistake has been corrected” in another. On Monday (November 23), 11 days after resigning from the top job, Huang appeared at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California, soon after the announcement. “Thank you all for a second chance.I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” he told a room full of employees, many of them cheering. The reversal is one of the most remarkable comebacks in business history. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to a blacklist which means the company can no longer receive Nvidia chips without a government licence.The allegations: On October 29, the New York Times reported that US intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government. The report said she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. It also said Trump was briefed about a year earlier but did not act. Later reports said China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China.After the report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with her. He likened it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said.However, on November 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair. “There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote, and he promised to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation. The board announced that investigation the same day. Overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, the board said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air. ”The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. When the Times reached him by phone, Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up, the report said. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal said that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting.By the next morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. Tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Senator Ron Wyden and Richard E. Neal announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Senator Tim Scott asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.Hours after the resignation, news agency Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Chief Marketing Officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026.Almost as soon as Huang was ousted, tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff began working on a comeback, as per comments on social media and several reports.For example, US President Donald Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” he said, adding that Huang had “learned a big lesson.” Trump also posted on Truth Social calling for Huang to be rehired.On Monday (November 23), he told CNBC he had been talking with the board and Huang, and that the board had been reasonable. “I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump said. He added that the US national security team does not believe Huang is a national security threat. Trump said he worked with Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to get Huang back.An Nvidia employee launched a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. By November 16, more than 206,000 names were on it. Signatories included Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and tech investor Gavin Baker. The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known. ”Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called Huang “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry. He said it was up to Nvidia’s board to decide what happened next. On Wednesday, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey called for Huang to return at the Times’ DealBook summit. He said that getting rid of Huang only benefited China.Amid immense support, Huang broke his silence on X, saying sorry for “serious mistakes” in his personal life and promised to cooperate with the board’s investigation. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.On the day after Huang resigned, the board said it was hiring an executive search firm and had not yet approached any candidates. Last Tuesday, board chair Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”On the day Huang’s resignation was announced, Nvidia shares fell as much as 14.35% in intraday trading. At the low, that wiped out about $600 billion in value. The stock ultimately closed down 4.34%.By Friday, November 20, Nvidia lost its position as the third-most valuable US company, after a prolonged selloff pushed its market capitalisation below that of Google parent Alphabet, reshuffling the rankings of America's biggest technology companies. Apple retained the top position with a valuation of approximately $5.08 trillion, followed by Microsoft at $3.72 trillion. Alphabet moved into third place, pushing Nvidia to fourth.Not just employees, but markets cheered Huang’s return. By the close on Monday, the S&P 500 had gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. The rebound recovered roughly half of the S&P’s losses from last week and more than half of the Nasdaq’s. Nvidia shares rose more than 30% to close at $165.05. The company gained approximately $1 trillion in value with Huang becoming roughly $34 billion to $36.6 billion richer in a single day.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO. His exit, triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, gripped the business and political worlds for two weeks. His return is likely to send more shockwaves through the tech industry and the halls of power. The reversal is one of the most remarkable comebacks in business history.

Article Title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, but it won't be like last time
Article Text:
Same CEO, different Nvidia

Huang's board kept learning the truth from everyone but him

Behind the personal scandal is a national security case that has not closed

The staff who cheered him have heard the other stories too

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe Jensen Huang deserves a second chance as CEO of Nvidia? Yes, everyone deserves a second chance. No, his past actions disqualify him. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nvidia's announcement bringing back Jensen Huang has all the parts you would expect. There is a unanimous vote, a warm line from the chair calling Huang "the right person to lead Nvidia", and a humble quote from Huang thanking his family. Then the last two paragraphs change the subject. They cover the investigation into him that will "proceed to conclusion", a new national security committee, a compliance chief who will not report to him, and the government inquiries Nvidia will keep cooperating with.It is an unusual way to welcome back a founder, and it says a lot about the job he is returning to.The people who work for him kept it simpler. When Huang walked into Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday, employees were waiting on the staircases and balconies, many of them filming on their phones. He had swapped the leather jacket for a fleece, took the hugs and the applause, and made them a promise: "Thank you all for the second chance. I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around." It was the welcome the statement had left out.They were the easy audience. The day before, he had spent several hours with a board that had pushed him out over his honesty, and that still had questions about what else he had not told it.When Huang left, the board was clear about why. Chair Harvey Jones told staff the resignation had been accepted over Huang's "lack of candor". The affairs were the trigger, but the charge was about what the CEO had told his own board, and when.The record explains the concern. Nvidia's general counsel reportedly had to go to Huang's home after a news report and ask him whether it was true. The board learned about a second relationship, with a vice president who reported directly to him, from The New York Times, and about a third, with another employee, from a later report.Each time, someone other than Huang told the board first. His only public account, posted after he resigned, admitted "serious mistakes" in his personal life without saying what they were.So when Nvidia said directors were now "satisfied" with his candour, that was the heart of the decision. According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang used Sunday's meeting to tell the board about affairs beyond those already reported. The Journal did not say how many, or with whom. He expressed remorse, and directors discussed his lack of transparency.Then they voted unanimously to reinstate him.The board can say it finally heard the truth from Huang himself. It can also be asked why that took a resignation, a week of headlines and a meeting about his comeback.The known relationships are serious enough. One was with Alice Huang (no relation), a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials have linked to Chinese intelligence. Two were with people at Nvidia, which bars managers from relationships with subordinates for an obvious reason: a boss holds power over the people who report to him. Whether any of the newly disclosed affairs involved staff is not yet known, and the board's investigation is still open.The board was not weighing all this alone.Nvidia's statement credits only "senior levels of the United States government". Trump has been less discreet, saying he spoke to the board himself and "convinced" it. He also asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and the directors, and Vance spent the weekend on calls with them. The New York Times reported that the administration offered two assurances: that it did not see Huang as a national security threat, and that he was not facing criminal charges.The White House makes no secret of its role. "President Trump was totally involved," communications director Steven Cheung said. Trump himself told the Journal that as Nvidia's stock plummeted, "the conditions became more favorable", and after the vote he called Huang "a Great Patriot and National Treasure".There is also Trump's own portfolio to consider. His disclosures show he bought Nvidia shares in September and may have held about 370,000 of them by the end of the month. By one estimate, that stake rose by roughly $15 million on the day Huang got his job back. Vance has said independent advisers manage the president's money. What those advisers did between Huang's exit and his return will not be known until Trump's October and November trades are disclosed.Even Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, one of the investors who wanted the door kept open for Huang, had warned against political pressure forcing a decision before directors knew what had happened. A week later, the board had fresh disclosures, an unfinished investigation and the White House telling it there was nothing to worry about.It agreed the same day.The board's decision was about Huang's honesty. What Washington cares about is the chips.Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company and grew by buying restricted Nvidia hardware, reportedly more than $4 billion worth. Investigators say Alice Huang used industry contacts and shell companies to reach 240,000 chips banned for export to China. Nvidia itself reportedly introduced her to Alibaba in 2022. The New York Times has reported that US officials concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during the relationship. It also reported that Huang was unmasked in US surveillance without ever receiving a defensive briefing, the warning normally given to someone a foreign intelligence service is targeting.The warnings were not new. Senator Tom Cotton asked the Commerce Department to investigate Megaspeed in October 2025, and Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for eight months before barring her from the country. The spy claims themselves remain unproven. China calls them a smear, Singapore says it never investigated her for espionage, and Megaspeed says she left in August 2025 and denies wrongdoing.The export questions stand either way. The Justice Department is running a criminal investigation into Megaspeed. The rules have tightened in the meantime. The Commerce Department has issued a new rule on remote access to advanced chips through overseas data centres, and Nvidia has said it is not shipping its Hopper data centre chips, including the H200, to China. On the day Nvidia's board voted, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the inquiry into Alice Huang and her former firm was ongoing. "Nvidia chips, they are the jewel," he said.So the government that told Nvidia's board Huang posed no threat is still investigating where his company's chips ended up.The rest of Washington is not finished with him either. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Huang should not return at all. Huang now faces a closed-door interview with House committees on December 1, and Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott wants him two days later. Shareholders have sued over Nvidia's disclosures, the SEC is reportedly examining its accounting, California's attorney general has served a subpoena, and Moody's has cut its outlook on the company, citing governance.Inside Nvidia, the board has rebuilt the structure around him. Jones, a director since 1993, is the company's first-ever chair and is keeping the role. A National Security and Export Control Committee of independent directors will oversee trade compliance, and a Chief Compliance Officer will report to a board committee rather than to the CEO.Huang sits on neither.Monday made it clear how much of Nvidia still belongs to Huang. Employees on three floors chanted his first name as he made his way in. With a hand on his heart, he admitted he had made terrible mistakes and joked that nobody had given him a computer yet.The welcome was loud, but it was not unanimous. According to Wired, some current and former employees saw his exit as a rare chance to change the "one team" culture he built over three decades, one in which, they say, challenging leadership was discouraged and abusive behaviour tolerated. Most spoke anonymously, fearing a backlash from colleagues.One wrote internally that everyone agreed mistakes had been made, and "the question is what we are ready to forgive". Another said they would stop doing HR trainings if he came back.Even the public show of support comes with an asterisk. The Stand With Jensen petition claims more than 10,000 Nvidia employees among its signatories, out of roughly 49,000 staff and 18,000 contractors. One employee told colleagues they had found 75 suspicious names in an hour of checking.The loyalty is real, and much of it is earned. Supporters credit Huang with keeping bureaucracy down, staying available to staff and making Nvidia feel like a family, and his AI bets have made many long-serving employees rich. Others are torn. Jason Sequeira, a longtime engineering leader, wrote publicly that he could not decide whether he wanted Huang back. He set the case for a second chance against the danger of making exceptions for powerful leaders.That danger is what a New York Times investigation, published while Huang was out of the job, puts on the record. In 2024, he said he would rather "torture you into greatness" than fire people, calling it tongue-in-cheek.Drawing on more than a dozen current and former staff and hundreds of pages of court records over 20 years, the investigation describes executives berated in front of their teams, people mocked for spending time with their children, and violent threats, including one about ripping off a subordinate's arms and beating the person to death with them. Huang reportedly told staff they had become too rich to be motivated by money, which left humiliation. Nvidia paid more than $1 million to settle confidentially with a former head of HR who said he was fired after confronting Huang. A former company lawyer said in a lawsuit that the conduct sent him for emergency medical help for severe anxiety.Neither settlement included an admission of wrongdoing, and Huang's spokesperson called the HR chief's account "fabrications" from a fired employee.For other employees, the bigger worry is accountability. Some told Wired they wanted to know whether the board would hold Huang to account for allegedly misleading directors about his affairs.They have also watched Nvidia cope without him. Colette Kress ran the earnings call, raised the growth outlook and reportedly handed out pay raises and extra equity. Investors still backed Huang, sending the shares up about 31% on his return, though the stock remains roughly a third below its October peak.So "a better CEO" comes with a fairly specific brief. It means telling his board things before they surface elsewhere. It means a company where senior staff are not threatened in meetings, concerns can be raised without fear, and the rule on relationships with subordinates applies at the top too. And it means giving answers under oath in Washington, to lawmakers who did not want him back.The AI boom has concentrated an unusual share of the world's computing power, market value and strategic leverage in a few companies and the founders who run them. Washington treats Nvidia's chips as a national asset, investors treat Huang as close to irreplaceable, and many of his staff see the company and the man as one.Last week, all of them pushed in the same direction.The usual checks on a chief executive are a board, a code of conduct, an internal investigation and the threat of being shown the door. They were built for companies that matter, not for companies a government considers too important to be without their founder. Nvidia's board used every one of them and still ended up where the White House and the market wanted it to.That leaves a question bigger than Nvidia: when a company becomes this central to a country's economy and security, who is still in a position to hold the person running it to account?
Article Summary: Huang's board kept learning the truth from everyone but him. Behind the personal scandal is a national security case that has not closed. The staff who cheered him have heard the other stories too. The board can say it finally heard the truth. It can also be asked why that took a resignation, a week of headlines and a meeting about his comeback.

Article Title: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt agrees with Meta AI head Alexandr Wang’s ‘dangerous’ superintelligence warning, says ‘extraordinary and…’
Article Text:
Google ex-CEO Eric Schmidt

Why Alexandr Wang says ‘superintelligence is arriving’

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has publicly backed the stark warning from Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang regarding the rapid rise of artificial intelligence (AI), or Superintelligence, calling Wang’s assessment “correct. ” Schmidt’s endorsement follows a detailed post shared by Wang on social media platform X (formerly Twitter), in which the Meta AI leader warned that the world may already be stepping into the era of superintelligence. Writing amid debate across the tech industry over how fast AI is advancing, Wang cautioned that the coming year could prove decisive in determining whether ultra-powerful AI systems benefit humanity or spiral into outcomes humans struggle to control.While acknowledging AI’s ability to speed up scientific and economic progress, Wang stressed that people must stay actively involved in steering society’s future rather than quietly handing it over to machines. Schmidt reshared Wang’s long note, saying: “Extraordinary, and correct, from Alexandr Wang”.Schmidt is among those industry leaders who have backed AI technology for good but has repeatedly warned about its dangers if humans do not control it.Schmidt pointed to scientific research as an area where AI could help, saying that professors, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers can work alongside AI agents under human supervision for AI-assisted problem solving. However, he blamed technology companies for failing to highlight positives of the technology.“Our industry does a terrible job of marketing our benefits. We talk about all the negatives without talking [about] the positives, and people are much more likely to index their minds on the negatives,” Schmidt said.In his post, Wang declared that “superintelligence is arriving,” arguing that recent breakthroughs show machines are quickly catching up to, and in some areas surpassing, the highest levels of human intellect. As proof of how dramatically the landscape is shifting, Wang pointed to the reported proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems. Calling it an intellectual feat unlike anything humanity has ever seen, Wang said the breakthrough highlighted the power of what he termed an “alien mind” that humans do not fully comprehend.Wang noted that solving elite mathematical problems demands more sheer intellectual horsepower than most everyday tasks handled by software engineers, cybersecurity specialists, or business professionals. As AI capabilities have grown, practical roadblocks have shrunk, making modern models highly effective across coding, cybersecurity, and other industries.Because of this shift, Wang expects AI to become the primary driver of progress across nearly every field of human activity, essentially outperforming top human experts along the way.Wang also questioned whether humanity could maintain control over unconstrained recursive self-improvement or a superintelligence 1,000 times smarter than people in every discipline.
Article Summary: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt has publicly backed the stark warning from Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang regarding the rapid rise of artificial intelligence. Schmidt’s endorsement follows a detailed post shared by Wang on social media platform X (formerly Twitter), in which the Meta AI leader warned that the world may already be stepping into the era of superintelligence.

Article Title: Back in Nvidia headquarters as CEO, Jensen Huang makes a promise to employees after thanking them for giving second chance; says: I will be ...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang reinstatement followed by weeks of turmoil

Celebrations at Nvidia headquarters as Jensen Huang is back as CEO

Questions emerge over Nvidia board’s handling of crisis

The investigation into Jensen Huang will still run its course

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The return of Jensen Huang as the CEO of Nvidia was met with cheers, chants and celebrations at the company’s headquarters, according to a report by CNBC. The employees were very happy when the board reinstated Huang as the CEO. For the uninitiated, Huang resigned on November 12, ending a 33-year run as CEO. His exit came days after Nvidia said it would investigate reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Those reports linked him to a woman US officials believe was recruited by China's spy agency. CFO Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO.The report further suggests that Huang was greeted by employees chanting his first name across the three floors of Nvidia headquarters. Addressing the staff, Huang thanked everyone for standing by him during the turbulent time. “Thank you all for the second chances,” Huang told employees. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”The leadership shake-up at Nvidia started after reported of Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, surfaced online triggering renewed scrutiny over the illegal smuggling of restricted Nvidia chips to China.Huang also acknowledged the affair in a note to Nvidia employees and stepped down from the position of CEO on November 12.Subsequent reports from Reuters and The New York Times said the Nvidia chief had relationships with two employees, including one who directly reported to him. The developments sparked intense attention on the company and its leadership at a time when Nvidia remains one of the most influential players in the global artificial intelligence industry.As reported by CNBC, the Nvidia employees celebrated the return of the company’s long-time leader. Cupcakes were seen at the headquarters with a ‘Jensen is back’ and were distributed to the employees. A person familiar with the celebrations at Nvidia told CNBC that many of the employees at the company were frustrated how the events unfolded in the past two weeks. The source further added that the company’s all-hand meeting held last week proved to be a turning point in shaping employee sentiment.The report added that an internally circulated side-by-side image compared one of Huang’s all-hands meetings with a more recent employee gathering that featured a group of executives and board members on stage, highlighting the contrast in leadership styles.Attention is now shifting toward Nvidia’s board of directors, which had indicated only last week that Huang would not be returning to the top job. A former Nvidia employee quoted by CNBC said the board could face criticism for reversing its position so quickly.“It’s embarrassing for the board,” the former employee said, adding that some directors could potentially step down or be replaced. The former staffer also said many employees felt the board had acted too hastily in pushing Huang out.Huang's return does not end the probe. A committee made up only of independent directors, working with independent counsel, is looking into the foreign intelligence reports. The board said the investigation will proceed to its conclusion. Huang has said he fully supports it and will cooperate.Nvidia is also adding new layers of oversight. The board recently set up a National Security and Export Control Committee, again made up only of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. It is bringing in counsel with national security experience, who will hire specialist advisers of their own. The company has also started a search for a new Chief Compliance Officer, who will report to the board's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations. Huang and general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to answer questions from US House committees behind closed doors on December 1 and 2.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang was reinstated as the CEO of Nvidia on December 1. Huang resigned on November 12, ending a 33-year run as CEO. His exit came after Nvidia said it would investigate reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Reports linked him to a woman US officials believe was recruited by China's spy agency.

Article Title: How Bees helped engineers solve what has been regarded as Solar panels’ biggest design flaw since their invention
Article Text:
Representative Image

Why flat solar panels are regarded as one of the biggest design flaws since their invention

How the honeycomb design helps solar panels recover reflected light

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

How the prototype could fit curved surfaces

Solar panels lose some sunlight to reflection. The problem becomes more pronounced when sunlight strikes a flat panel at a shallow angle. It has been regarded as one of solar panels’ biggest design flaws since their invention. Engineers at the Korea Electrotechnology Research Institute found a way to recover some of that light by borrowing the hexagonal pattern of a honeycomb. They built a three-dimensional solar module with recessed cells that can redirect light reflected from one cell onto another.In a study published in Advanced Materials Technologies, the researchers reported that the honeycomb structure produced 28% more power than flat cells in their tests. The team also built a flexible support frame that lets the modules fit curved surfaces, such as the sides of buildings.Light can reflect at two points in a conventional solar panel. Some of it bounces off the protective glass, while some of the light that passes through the glass reflects off the solar cells underneath. The researchers estimated that these two effects account for a combined loss of about 6% to 8% of incoming light even when it strikes a conventional flat panel head-on.The amount reflected depends on the angle at which the light hits the panel. In the researchers’ calculations, reflection from the protective materials rose more sharply once incoming light reached about 60 degrees from a line perpendicular to the surface. On a flat panel, that reflected light can travel away from the cells.The researchers mounted three silicon solar cells on the sloping sides of each recess. When light reflects off one cell, it can strike another cell facing it. That gives the module another chance to absorb light that would otherwise escape. The team tested recesses with cells tilted at 40 and 60 degrees to examine how the tilt affected light recapture and power output.The honeycomb shape gave the team a way to repeat those recesses across a module. The engineers arranged six recessed units into a hexagon, allowing groups of units to fit closely together with little space between them.The researchers used a 3D-printed polymer frame that flexes between the recessed units while holding the cells at fixed angles within each unit. They linked the units with wavy copper strips embedded in a stretchable resin. The strips can extend as the frame bends, keeping the units electrically connected.The team identified curved building surfaces and indoor energy harvesting as possible applications and said further research would be needed to assess how the modules perform in practical use.
Article Summary: Solar panels lose some sunlight to reflection. The problem becomes more pronounced when sunlight strikes a flat panel at a shallow angle. Engineers found a way to recover some of that light by borrowing the hexagonal pattern of a honeycomb. They built a three-dimensional solar module with recessed cells that can redirect light.

The future of a $1.6 billion data centre proposal in Menomonie, western Wisconsin, remains unclear as the city’s new mayor says he will not negotiate any development agreements with the firm behind the project. Previous mayor Randy Knaack, after listening to concerns about the project from members of the community, banned the data center project. This comes even though the city council has already annexed and rezoned about 320 acres of farmland for it. This is similar to another data centre dispute involving homeowner Jerry Zelenka who turned down a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC). The money was offered for a proposed power line that would cross his property in Fredonia, Wisconsin, to supply electricity to a planned data centre in nearby Port Washington.After last year’s controversy, the Menomonie City Council has been trying to win back public trust. It has held several public meetings in recent months to gather community input. It is also considering new data centre restrictions, which would add to the ordinance passed in January.This summer, the city’s new mayor, Matthew Crowe, issued a press release saying the representatives of Balloonist, the company behind the proposal, had contacted city staff.That could suggest the company is willing to revisit the project. Crowe said he declined to meet them “to avoid being unduly influenced”.Residents’ push to stop the project has largely worked, but its fate is far from settled, as per a report by The Guardian published earlier this month. Officially, the development is paused. Balloonist, however, still owns the land.In September last year, mayor Randy Knaack banned the construction of the data centre, and later in his “Mayor’s Report”, the mayor drafted a memo on September 17, and had the city administrator send it to Balloonist LLC.“In the document, I stated that I am not currently interested in pursuing a tax increment district or development agreement as the chief executive officer of Menomonie,” Knaack said, adding that after hearing the community’s concerns, “the data center is now on pause.”Another data centre dispute in the state centres on homeowner Jerry Zelenka. He turned down a $131,000 offer from American Transmission Company (ATC). The money was offered for a proposed power line that would cross his property in Fredonia, Wisconsin, to supply electricity to a planned data centre in nearby Port Washington.Zelenka, 75, said the latest plan would clear mature trees, demolish six buildings and put a 130-foot transmission tower near his driveway. He and his wife bought the land in 1990. According to Zelenka, ATC’s latest proposal follows an earlier application that the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin deemed incomplete. The company has since filed a new application with revised plans and routes.He said a stretch of about 1,000 feet long and 75 feet wide would be cleared of trees and vegetation. The trees include cedar, oak, ash, elm and black walnut. The project would also require removing a shed, chicken coop, hog barn, antique barn, garage and machine shed.“The point is that everything from that fence all the way to the road is clear-cut,” Zelenka said. “And after they clear-cut it, then they want to spray herbicide and just kill everything between my house and the highway.”The tower and high-voltage lines would also change the property’s surroundings, which could affect its value.ATC has offered $81,000 for the property impacts, plus a one-time $50,000 payment if he signs an agreement now. Zelenka said the compensation would not cover the cost of replacing the buildings or properly account for the loss in the property’s value. He also objected to the extra payment being tied to signing immediately.“You know, the bribe in a sense is that if I were to sign up now, they’re offering $50,000 more,” Zelenka said.He said moving is not a realistic option for him and his 73-year-old wife, who has advanced Parkinson’s disease. The couple built their home after buying the land in the winter of 1990, spending nine months on the house while living in a shed.

The city’s new mayor says he will not negotiate any development agreements with the firm behind the project. Previous mayor Randy Knaack, after listening to concerns about the project from members of the community, banned the data center project. This comes even though the city council has already annexed and rezoned about 320 acres of farmland for it.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer, bringing an end to a turbulent period which witnessed chief Colette Kress lead the AI chipmaker as interim CEO for 11 days. According to a CNBC report, along with Huang’s return, Nvidia also confirmed that Kress will continue in her role as chief financial officer, signalling the board’s continued confidence in one of the company’s longest-serving senior executives. The return of Jensen Huang came after he stepped down earlier this month following revelations related to extramarital relationships. The announcement sparked a strong market reaction, with Nvidia shares surging 31% on Monday while the Nasdaq gained more than 6%, reflecting investor enthusiasm for the comeback of the company’s co-founder and long-time leader.The board accepted Huang’s resignation on November 11 and appointed Kress, 59, as interim CEO. Huang, 63, resigned following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia shares jumped 31% on Monday and the Nasdaq rose more than 6% after the announcement, and employees cheered Huang as he returned to the office.Kress joined Nvidia as finance chief in September 2013, after stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.She holds about 4.775 million shares, worth roughly $778 million at Monday’s close. As CFO she oversees the balance sheet of a company that is financing many of the infrastructure deals behind the AI buildout, arrangements that have raised concerns about circular financing and exposure to a slowdown.While Huang has returned as CEO, president and board director with immediate effect, Nvidia said Kress will remain CFO. The 59-year-old executive, who joined Nvidia in September 2013 after leadership roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments, took charge of the company during one of the most challenging periods in its history.Kress currently holds approximately 4.775 million Nvidia shares directly and indirectly, giving her a stake valued at about $778 million based on Monday’s closing price. Her interim leadership role put her at the centre of Nvidia’s efforts to reassure investors, employees and customers amid uncertainty surrounding Huang’s departure.During Nvidia’s first earnings call following Huang’s resignation, Kress attempted to calm market concerns by raising the company’s fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to roughly 75%, up from an earlier estimate of 70%.She repeatedly stressed that operations remained on track and characterised the situation as “business as usual.” In media appearances, Kress said customer demand for Nvidia’s AI products continued to rise and that major clients remained committed to the company despite the leadership upheaval. At an all-hands employee meeting after Huang’s exit, she struck an optimistic tone, encouraging staff to focus on the future and highlighting upcoming pay increases.Not everyone shared the criticism. According to CNBC, one former Nvidia employee praised Kress for handling the crisis with “skill and grace” and helping reassure both employees and industry partners during a period of uncertainty.The person also expressed confidence that Kress would remain a key member of Nvidia’s leadership team after Huang’s return, describing her as a “fantastic CFO” who retains Huang’s trust.In the official announcement confirming his reinstatement, Huang publicly thanked Kress for leading the company during his absence. “I am grateful for Colette leading NVIDIA during this period,” Huang said. The statement appears to settle speculation over Kress’ future at the company, with Nvidia formally confirming that she will continue as CFO while Huang resumes control of the AI chip giant.For investors, the board’s decision restores the executive who has led Nvidia through its transformation into one of the world’s most valuable companies. For Kress, it means a return to overseeing the finances of the company she helped guide through a brief but highly scrutinised leadership crisis.Huang's return does not end the probe. A committee made up only of independent directors, working with independent counsel, is looking into the foreign intelligence reports. The board said the investigation will proceed to its conclusion. Huang has said he fully supports it and will cooperate.Nvidia is also adding new layers of oversight. The board recently set up a National Security and Export Control Committee, again made up only of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. It is bringing in counsel with national security experience, who will hire specialist advisers of their own. The company has also started a search for a new Chief Compliance Officer, who will report to the board's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with ongoing government investigations. Huang and general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to answer questions from US House committees behind closed doors on December 1 and 2.
Article Summary: Colette Kress will continue in her role as chief financial officer. The return of Jensen Huang came after he stepped down earlier this month following revelations related to extramarital relationships. Nvidia shares jumped 31% on Monday and the Nasdaq rose more than 6% after the announcement.
