Article Title: Nvidia's U-turn on Jensen Huang: How the 'ousted' CEO returned in 11 days, what changed the board's mind, and why his troubles are not over
Article Text:
Ousted, then reinstated in 11 days

Nvidia's board says the candour problem behind Huang's exit is resolved

The US government moved from caution to support for Huang within days

Investors wanted Huang back, though not all wanted the board to rush

Jensen Huang returns with the export-control questions around Nvidia still open

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

On November 17, Nvidia chair Harvey Jones opened the company's earnings call with a line that seemed to settle the matter: the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO". Five days later, the same board voted unanimously to bring him back. Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia's president, CEO and board director on November 23, 11 days after he resigned from the company he co-founded in 1993.Nvidia's explanation is brief. Directors say meetings with Huang left them satisfied with his candour and his ability to lead. They add that input from senior US government officials gave them confidence his return carries no national security risk. The statement leaves out what happened in the days between those two board positions. In that time, Nvidia's stock had its worst day in nearly two years, the US President publicly asked for Huang back, and the company's own investors disagreed over how fast the board should move.Huang stepped down on November 12. On October 29, The New York Times had reported that US officials concluded Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was a Chinese intelligence asset. On November 7, the Financial Times reported that the US believed the relationship was romantic.On November 11, The New York Times reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang admitted infidelity in a note to employees on November 8, and CFO Colette Kress stepped in as interim CEO.The word the board chose matters most. At an all-hands meeting on November 18, Jones told employees the board had accepted Huang's resignation because of his "lack of candor". The stated reason was how open Huang had been with the board, more than the relationships themselves.The timeline shows where that concern came from. On October 29, Huang described Nvidia's dealings with Megaspeed as "completely normal". The New York Times later reported that on the night of November 7, general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang's home and asked him directly whether the reports were true. Huang said they were. On November 8, the board said it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia's secrets had been compromised, and it opened an investigation.The November 23 statement speaks to the same concern. Nvidia says directors held "a series of discussions and meetings" with Huang, after which they were satisfied with his candour. Huang had also made the first move in public. On November 17, he posted on X that he had made "serious mistakes" and offered to return if the board felt it served shareholders. Semafor reported the same day that three directors were already pushing for his comeback.The national security question was harder to settle inside a boardroom, and the board did not try to settle it alone. Its statement credits "senior levels of the United States government" for its confidence, without naming the officials.The intelligence picture has never been clear-cut. On October 30, China's foreign ministry called the spy report "groundless speculation". On November 12, Singapore's home affairs ministry said it had investigated Alice Huang, but not for espionage. US Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had reached no conclusion on whether she was a spy, and CNN reported that the intelligence did not prove she was one. On November 13, The Washington Post reported that a memo by Marco Rubio was based on a CIA report that he had recast more assertively.The politics moved in Huang's favour over the same days. On November 12, President Donald Trump called the developments "horrible" and "sad", and he later suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook as a successor. On November 15, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the board needed "a dramatic shakeup". On November 16, Trump said he would not mind Huang returning. On November 20, he said he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. "On November 22, Trump wrote on Truth Social: "I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A." Bessent, who had wanted an outside hire, said in a TV interview the same day: "I said they should go to the outside, but he's on the outside now." Nvidia's filing with the US securities regulator dates the board's decision to November 22 as well.The market pressure was hard to miss. On November 20, Nvidia shares fell nearly 14% to $125.53, their worst day since January 2025. By then the stock had lost about $2.7 trillion in market value since its October 6 peak. On November 18, Moody's lowered its outlook on Nvidia's Aa1 credit rating to stable. By November 16, a "Stand With Jensen" petition had passed 178,000 signatures, and Elon Musk was among the tech figures publicly backing Huang.The most prominent investor push was more measured than the petition. On November 14, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker asked the board for a slow, deliberate CEO search that left room for Huang's return. Their firms held about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock between them. They did not ask for him to be reinstated straight away. Speaking at a conference on November 16, Gerstner warned against political pressure from either side pushing the board to act "before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done".The board's own investigation into Huang has not finished, so he returns before that inquiry reaches a conclusion.The business itself held up in his absence. On the November 17 earnings call, Kress raised Nvidia's growth outlook. Even so, shares jumped more than 25% in premarket trading on November 23 after the announcement. That still left them below the $166.19 close on the day Huang resigned.The bigger questions Nvidia now faces are about where its chips ended up, and most of them lead back to Huang. On November 18, The New York Times reported that Megaspeed bought more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips, with Alibaba as a customer and backer. The Information reported that Nvidia had introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang in 2022. On November 16, the US Justice Department and the Commerce Department announced that the Justice Department was conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed. On November 13, Bessent said "several agencies" had favoured putting Megaspeed on the US entity list for months. On November 17, Nvidia said it was not shipping Hopper data centre products, including H200 processors, to China.This is where the troubles are not yet behind Huang. The relationship that led to his exit is tied to a company now under criminal investigation, and that company was a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. The board's assurance on national security rests on input from officials it has not named. The investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort is still running, and he will lead Nvidia while it reaches its findings.Huang says he will cooperate with it.Nvidia's own steps show it expects more scrutiny. A new National Security and Export Control Committee, made up only of independent directors, will oversee trade compliance and national security risks. Nvidia is also hiring a Chief Compliance Officer, who will report to the board's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.The calendar outside the company is full too. Huang is due for a closed-door interview with US House committees on December 1, and general counsel Tim Teter is due on December 2. Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott has asked Huang to testify on December 3. The Wall Street Journal reported on November 17 that the SEC was investigating Nvidia's disclosures. On November 19, California Attorney General Rob Bonta served the company a subpoena. Jones stays on as board chair, and Kress continues as CFO.

Directors say meetings with Huang left them satisfied with his candour and his ability to lead. They add that input from senior US government officials gave them confidence his return carries no national security risk.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos made two big donations in 2026, what makes the stock gifts 'historic' is that both go to the Day 1 of ...
Article Text:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

Jeff Bezos donated nearly $200 million donated in November

Where the shares went

More than $600 million worth of stock donated this year

A deadline approaching

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What the Day 1 network does

How his giving compares to his ex-wife MacKenzie Scott

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has donated more than $600 million worth of Amazon shares in 2026, but two of his most recent gifts stand out for a unique reason: some of the stock was acquired on Julu 5, 1994, the day he incorporated the company that would eventually become Amazon. According to a report by Fortune, the shares effectively date back to the company’s ‘Day 1’, making them among the earliest Amazon shares still linked to Bezos’ holdings. The Amazon founder and executive chair donated 674,088 shares on Nov. 12 and 97,404 more the next day, according to a Nov. 16 SEC filing. Forbes valued the 771,492 shares at $198.9 million, based on Amazon’s $257.75 close that day.According to securities filings cited by Fortune, Bezos donated 674,088 Amazon shares on November 12 and another 97,404 shares on November 13. Based on Amazon's closing share price of $257.75 on November 16, Forbes estimated the value of the combined 771,492 shares at roughly $198.9 million.Part of the donation, worth about $25 million, went to the Bezos Earth Fund. The fund also filed notice of its intention to sell the shares, according to SEC filings.What makes this particular donation noteworthy is that the shares were originally acquired on July 5, 1994, the same day Bezos incorporated the company that later became Amazon, nearly three years before the retailer's public market debut in 1997.The smaller gift, worth about $25 million, went to the Bezos Earth Fund Foundation, which Bezos founded. It filed a notice of its intent to sell the shares. Bezos acquired those shares on July 5, 1994, the day he incorporated the company that became Amazon, almost three years before its 1997 IPO. The filings don’t name the recipient of the larger gift. The November gifts follow two earlier rounds: more than 1.25 million shares in May and 415,580 in August, worth about $323 million and $107 million at the Nov. 16 close. In all, Bezos has donated at least 2.44 million shares this year, worth about $629.1 million at that price.Day 1 Academies, the nonprofit behind his network of tuition-free preschools, received at least 450,837 of those shares, 220,200 in May and 230,637 in August. With the Earth Fund, the two nonprofits he founded account for about 22.5% of this year’s donated shares. The filings describe the rest only as gifts to nonprofits. Even after the donations, Bezos directly held more than 878 million Amazon shares, worth about $226.4 billion per Forbes, so this year’s gifts are under 0.3% of the stake.The November transactions add to two earlier rounds of charitable stock gifts made by Bezos in 2026. Fortune reported that he donated more than 1.25 million Amazon shares in May and another 415,580 shares in August. Using Amazon's November 16 closing price, those donations were valued at approximately $323 million and $107 million respectively.Altogether, the Amazon founder has donated at least 2.44 million Amazon shares this year, worth about $629 million based on the same valuation.Bezos launched the Earth Fund in 2020 with a pledge to give away $10 billion by 2030. As of late September it had granted about $2.4 billion, meaning it would need to average roughly $1.8 billion a year to meet the goal, Fortune reported. On Nov. 19, the fund told Fortune it is committing more than $100 million to protect the Amazon rainforest through 15 new grants across South America. Day 1 Academies runs 38 Montessori-inspired preschools in underserved communities across six states and enrolled 2,456 students for 2026-27. They grew out of a $2 billion commitment Bezos announced in 2018, whose other arm, the Day 1 Families Fund, awarded $102.5 million to 32 groups in 2025.Day 1 Academies operates 38 tuition-free preschools across Arizona, Florida, Hawaii, Kentucky, Texas and Washington. According to its annual report, the network enrolled 2,456 students for the 2026-27 academic year. The schools were created through the Day 1 Fund, a $2 billion philanthropic commitment announced by Bezos in 2018 to support early childhood education and families experiencing homelessness. Another arm of the initiative, the Day 1 Families Fund, provides grants to organisations helping families move from homelessness into stable housing.Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, had given an estimated $4.7 billion through the end of 2025, 10th on Forbes’ list of top US philanthropists, with about $600 million of it in 2025. Bezos has said he plans to give away most of his fortune in his lifetime. He told CNN in 2022 that the hard part is working out how to do it “in a levered way.” His ex-wife, MacKenzie Scott, gave away $7.2 billion in 2025 alone, bringing her total since their 2019 divorce to $26.4 billion, Forbes estimates. That one year exceeded what Bezos and Sánchez Bezos have given in their lifetimes.
Article Summary: The Amazon founder and executive chair donated 674,088 shares on Nov. 12 and 97,404 more the next day, according to a Nov. 16 SEC filing. Forbes valued the 771,492 shares at $198.9 million, based on Amazon’s $257.75 close that day. Part of the donation, worth about $25 million, went to the Bezos Earth Fund. The fund also filed notice of its intention to sell the shares. The November transactions add to two earlier rounds of charitable stock gifts made by Bezos in 2026.

Article Title: Microsoft CFO Amy Hood, who was rejected twice and later joined the company without knowing salary, has advice for Gen Z: ‘I can’t believe I’m saying this but …’
Article Text:
Microsoft CFO Amy Hood

How Amy Hood’s career took shape

Microsoft rejected her twice

Why her advice matters for today’s graduates

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Amy Hood, the chief financial officer (CFO) of Microsoft, did not have a master plan for her career. As an economics undergraduate at Duke University in the 1990s, she could not have guessed she would one day hold the top finance job at one of the world’s biggest tech companies. For Hood, her career has looked more like a roller coaster than a ladder. That is the lesson she shared with the class of 2026 at Duke’s commencement ceremony. Her lesson comes at a delicate time when the tech industry is undergoing a transformation, and companies across the tech industry, Microsoft included, have cut thousands of roles in recent years as they restructure and invest more in artificial intelligence (AI).Hood graduated from Duke in 1994. She built her early career at Goldman Sachs and later earned an MBA from Harvard. Over time, she realised corporate banking was not how she wanted to spend the rest of her life. So she quit, without much of a plan for what came next. She told students in May: “As you start out, many successful careers are rarely—if ever—a straight line. Your next step doesn’t have to be a perfect one. It just has to be an opportunity.She found what seemed like the perfect reset: an internship with the National Park Service.“I thought, this is perfect. It’s a sign—I’ll get assigned to Yosemite or Yellowstone, someplace iconic. I’ll work outdoors, I’ll live somewhere beautiful, and feel the space and energy that nature provides,” Hood recalled. Instead, the then 30-year-old was sent to Alcatraz Island, which she described as “a prison on a rock”. It was nothing like what she had imagined, and she quit after a single day.Months later, after a long job search, a friend called and asked if she wanted to interview at Microsoft. She had already been rejected by the company twice. This time she landed a role in investor relations and accepted the offer without even asking about the salary. The gamble still paid off. Over the next decade, she rose steadily through the ranks and was named CFO in 2013.For many of today’s graduates, Hood’s winding road to the top may feel out of reach. Expectations are also out of step with the job market. Hood acknowledged the uncertainty facing Gen Z, however, she argued that many young workers are better prepared than they think. In her view, the bigger challenge is letting go of the idea that they must have everything figured out right away.“I can’t believe I’m saying this to some of the most accomplished young people on the planet, but maybe lower your bar a little. Be open that something may not be exactly right, but could turn out to be a perfect place to learn about yourself—what you like, what you don’t. All the steps matter, and it took me decades to figure that out,” she said.She also urged graduates to stay adaptable and curious in a world that is changing faster than it did for any earlier generation.“You will figure out who you are by stepping in and letting people push back, by doing things that scare you just a little, by raising your hand when you’re pretty sure you don’t have the right answer, and by taking a job that doesn’t make sense on paper but makes sense to you,” she told graduates.
Article Summary: Amy Hood, the chief financial officer (CFO) of Microsoft, did not have a master plan for her career. As an economics undergraduate at Duke University in the 1990s, she could not have guessed she would one day hold the top finance job at one of the world’s biggest tech companies. For Hood, her career has looked more like a roller coaster than a ladder.

Article Title: Arm 'locks in' CEO Rene Haas till 2033 as Nvidia hunts for Jensen Huang's successor; Haas says: I've never been more confident about...
Article Text:
Rene Haas picks Arm over Nvidia's top job (Picture: Reuters)

Rene Haas was Nvidia's most familiar outside pick for CEO

Nvidia's board has ruled out Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Arm Holdings has locked in chief executive Rene Haas until 2033, putting a lid on weeks of speculation that he could be Nvidia's next CEO. The 64-year-old has signed a new agreement with the Cambridge-headquartered chip designer. From December 1, he will also be vice chairman of SoftBank Group, Arm's majority owner. The announcement comes just over a week after reports said Nvidia's board had approached Haas in its search for a successor to co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned earlier this month."I've never been more confident about Arm's future," Haas said in a statement on Monday. "I believe deeply in our people, our strategy and the opportunity ahead. I'm incredibly proud of what we're building and wholly committed to realizing Arm's full potential for many years to come."Arm says AI is driving unprecedented demand for computing, and it wants to become an even bigger part of the infrastructure behind it.Few outsiders know Nvidia as well as Haas. He spent about seven years there and rose to vice president and general manager of its computing products business before leaving for Arm in 2013.Huang mentored him during that time. Haas is still close to Huang and to some of Nvidia's board members.Recruitment firm Heidrick & Struggles, hired by Nvidia's board, had started reaching out to candidates. The other names being discussed include AMD CEO Lisa Su, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, Nvidia vice president Ian Buck and CFO Colette Kress, who is currently interim CEO. The board has called any speculation about individual candidates premature.Haas did little to calm the talk last week when he called Huang "a legend" at a tech conference in Austin.Huang stepped down after 33 years in charge. His exit followed revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based client Megaspeed. US intelligence suspects she has ties to Chinese espionage. Reports also pointed to relationships with two Nvidia employees. Investigations are ongoing, and Huang has agreed to sit for transcribed interviews with three House committees in early December.He has since apologised for his conduct and said he would come back if the board asked. US President Donald Trump has publicly backed the idea. On Friday he said a smart company "would take this brilliant man back". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also said he would not oppose it. Nvidia chair Harvey Jones, however, has said the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO".So far the turmoil hasn't shown up in Nvidia's numbers. Its latest quarterly revenue doubled from a year earlier to $115.84 billion.Haas, meanwhile, has plenty on his plate. He became Arm's CEO in 2022 and took the company back to public markets the following year with a $65 billion Nasdaq listing. In March, Arm started selling its own AGI CPU chips, which put it in direct competition with some of its customers. A month later, Haas was put in charge of SoftBank's international business.Arm is valued at around $196 billion and licenses its chip designs to about 500 companies, including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm. Nvidia itself tried to buy Arm for $40 billion in 2020, but the deal collapsed over regulatory concerns.
Article Summary: Arm Holdings has locked in chief executive Rene Haas until 2033. The 64-year-old has signed a new agreement with the Cambridge-headquartered chip designer. From December 1, he will also be vice chairman of SoftBank Group, Arm's majority owner.

Article Title: LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero has a tip for Gen Z job seekers: Talk to someone who already…
Article Text:
LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero

LinkedIn CEO: AI is making the entry-level job market tougher

LinkedIn CEO says networking can be the fastest way to get a job

Why companies are hiring Gen Z for AI skills

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

AI is changing the job market, making it harder for fresh graduates to find entry-level jobs. But LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero believes Gen Z could also have an advantage as companies look for people who understand how to use AI at work. His advice to young job seekers, however, goes beyond learning new technology or sending out more applications. In an interview with Fortune recently, LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero said that building professional connections could be the fastest way to get hired. Instead of simply applying for jobs online, graduates should try to speak to someone already working at the company they want to join.Daniel Shapero described the current employment situation as a “frozen” job market, saying it is particularly difficult for people at the beginning of their careers. “It is a frozen job market, and that does make it tougher for people that are earlier in their career for sure,” Shapero told Fortune.However, he believes young candidates may have an advantage during job interviews as companies increasingly adopt artificial intelligence. Employers are looking for people who can understand new technology and use it to change the way businesses work.“There is a belief that people that are earlier, maybe they’re more attuned to the latest tech, and they understand how to use AI in their job,” Shapero said.He added that companies want to hire people who can help them “transform how the company operates.”This could create opportunities for Gen Z candidates, even as AI tools change the kind of work companies expect employees to do.Apart from building AI skills, Daniel Shapero has another suggestion for Gen Z job seekers: do not depend only on online applications. According to LinkedIn's data, the “fastest path” to landing a job is connecting with someone who already works at the company where a candidate wants to apply.This means reaching out to employees, building professional relationships and asking for introductions could be more useful than simply sending applications and waiting for a response. Shapero compared the job search process to raising money for a startup. Founders do not simply send emails to investors and hope someone agrees to fund their business. They try to meet people and build connections that can lead to introductions.“You wouldn’t just email all the VCs and hope that someone wrote you a check,” he said. “You would try to meet people. You would try to have those people introduce you to others.”His advice suggests that job seekers should approach their search in a similar way. Instead of relying entirely on application portals, they can identify people working in their target companies, start conversations and learn more about available opportunities.LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero is not the only business leader who believes younger workers could bring an advantage to companies adopting AI. Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise, a generative AI platform, said he is actively hiring entry-level candidates because they are more open to experimenting with new technology.“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries… They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities,” Chen told Fortune.He also believes younger employees can bring fresh thinking to businesses. “And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”The growing demand for AI-related skills could therefore give fresh graduates opportunities beyond traditional entry-level roles. Shapero also advised young candidates to consider jobs in industries they may not have initially thought about.“Sometimes your degree or your skills can be applied in areas that you maybe haven’t thought of,” he said adding “These days every company is a bit of a tech company.”
Article Summary: LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero believes Gen Z could have an advantage as companies look for people who understand how to use AI at work. His advice to young job seekers goes beyond learning new technology or sending out more applications. Instead of simply applying for jobs online, graduates should try to speak to someone already working at the company.
